rv.q: The result, directed by Scott Elliott, is a gorgeous mess.
The show is a mess that’s beyond repair.
This is a show not to miss as well as a likely instant landmark in the musical theater.
Therefore, more power to Black No More.

Despite the brilliant cast and the show's thematic daring, there is a palpable falloff in action during the second act as Ridley's book loses its satirical edge and humor, and slides into the melodramatic and preachy.
They both have many entrancing and effective elements, but Apparel is the more integrated and powerful piece.
But it was mostly…still just promising.
Unfortunately, despite its many powerful elements, the musical receiving its world premiere from Off-Broadway’s The New Group turns out to be something of a mess.
Black No More is certainly a daring attempt at something different, but it has structural issues -- it has at least three endings -- and it suffers from an excess of good intentions.
What does not get repeated is much of anything from Schuyler’s viciously satirical “Black No More.”

Sadly, it is all for naught. The music, lyrics, and book are so full of contrivances ― notwithstanding their lofty goal of criticizing racism ― I could not help laughing at the tragic obviousness of it all.
Black No More has absolutely nothing new to say about its themes. Nothing is illuminated, nothing lost or gained.

Despite Scott Elliot's irresolute direction, the musical's principals and ensemble negotiate John Ridley's book, Tariq Trotters' lyrics, and the music...with palpable passion and electrifying authenticity.
But it trips over itself a lot.

cn.t: An ambitious adaptation with powerhouse performances and inventive music from The Roots struggles with an unfocused book that undermines its satirical premise, resulting in mixed reviews despite its creative team's pedigree.
